title: A place to listen
blocks: p
A strong feeling can be a place to begin. It does not have to be the end of the inquiry.
p

This workbook invites you to explore what you notice before deciding what it means. Writing gives an impression somewhere to land: a page on which a feeling, a wish, a concern and an observable fact can exist without becoming the same thing.
p
Discernment, as used here, is a practice of attending, questioning, checking and revising. It is not a test of whether you are spiritual enough, calm enough or certain enough.
p

You may discover that a fear is pointing toward a real concern. You may notice that you want an answer so much that you have stopped asking questions. You may choose a boundary while remaining uncertain about someone else’s intentions.
quote
You can listen to yourself and still ask questions.
p
Begin with an ordinary, manageable question. You do not need to settle the largest question in your life to learn something useful.
note

Reflective writing, not a diagnostic tool or a method for proving psychic ability. For consequential decisions involving health, safety, law or money, include verifiable information and appropriate qualified advice. You may pause, skip a prompt or keep your writing private.

title: Use it in your own time
blocks: p
There is no schedule to keep and no correct pace. Read the teaching pages, choose the exercises that fit your question, and return when you have something new to consider.
bullets
For a first visit: choose one question on page 5, then work through the observation, fear and desire exercises.
For a decision: use the four lenses on page 15 and the decision lab on page 21.
After taking a step: return to pages 22-24 to review what happened.
For an ongoing practice: copy or revisit the check-in on page 26.
p

Keep the question small enough to examine. “Can I trust myself?” is a lifetime inquiry. “Do I want to accept this invitation, and what do I need to know first?” gives you something specific to work with.
p

Use a notebook for longer answers. The writing spaces in this PDF are fillable in compatible PDF readers, and the pages can also be printed. Save a personal copy before you begin. Some browser PDF viewers handle forms differently; check that your answers remain after saving and reopening.
note
Worked situations are hypothetical, not stories about Kali’s clients. No exercise can reliably label a feeling as fear, ego or intuition. You are developing a way to inquire, not a certainty score.
quote
Leave room on the page for “I don’t know yet.”

title: Four lenses, no verdict
blocks: p
Fear, ego, desire and intuition can overlap. These words are lenses for writing, not separate boxes into which every experience must fit.
p
Fear: what feels threatened, uncertain or potentially costly? Ask what the concern is responding to and what would address it.
p
Ego: what image of yourself are you trying to protect? Here, the word means investment in being seen a certain way, not a diagnosis or a bad part of you.
p
Desire: what do you want to happen? A wish can be honest and valuable without being evidence that the outcome will happen.
p
Intuition: what impression are you noticing before you can fully explain it? Treat the impression as a possibility to explore and compare with what you can observe.
p
A calm feeling is not proof of truth. Urgency is not proof of error. Neither bodily intensity nor a spiritual interpretation can establish another person’s motives.
quote
The useful question is not only “Which voice is this?” It is also “What does this ask me to notice, check or choose?”
field
Which lens do I tend to trust immediately? Which do I tend to dismiss?

title: Choose one question
blocks: p
Choose an ordinary situation you can explore without forcing an immediate resolution. Write the question in language you could return to a week from now.
field
The situation I want to explore is...
field
The question I am actually asking is...
field
What is mine to decide, and what belongs to someone else?
field
What would make this inquiry useful, even if I remain uncertain?
note
If the situation involves immediate danger, give practical safety needs priority. This workbook does not require you to stay in an unsafe situation or test a concern by taking a risk.

title: Observation is not interpretation
blocks: p
An observation describes something you experienced or could point to. An interpretation explains it. Both belong on the page, but keeping them separate creates room to examine your conclusion.
p

Observation: “My friend has not replied to the message I sent yesterday.”
Interpretation: “They are angry with me.”
Feeling: “I feel unsettled.”
Desire: “I want reassurance that we are okay.”
p
The interpretation may be right, partly right or wrong. The observation alone does not settle it. Other possibilities include a busy day, a missed notification or a wish to respond later.
p

Watch for words such as always, obviously, everyone and definitely. They can signal that an explanation has begun to feel like a fact. You do not have to ban those words; simply ask what supports them.
bullets
What happened, in the most specific language I can use?
What did I feel or notice in myself?
What explanation did I add?
What other explanation still fits the available facts?
quote
A sentence can feel convincing before it has been checked.

title: What happened / what I added
blocks: p
Use your chosen question. Give each part its own space. Describe another person’s observable actions without claiming to know their inner experience.
field
What I observed or experienced...
field
The meaning I immediately gave it...
field
Another explanation that also fits...
field
What I could check, and what I cannot currently know...

title: Notice the body, leave meaning open
blocks: p
You may notice a tight stomach, an impulse to speak, a wish to leave, or a sudden sense of ease. You can record that experience without making it prove a conclusion.
p

Try describing the sensation before naming its cause: “My shoulders lifted” leaves a different kind of space than “My body knows they are lying.” The first is an observation. The second makes a claim that needs examination.
p
If you want to pause, look around the room, change your position or put the page aside. You do not need to close your eyes, control your breathing or make yourself calm in order to use this workbook.
field
What am I noticing in my body or attention, without explaining it?
field
What was happening just before I noticed it? What else may be relevant?
note
A sensation deserves attention. Its meaning can remain open. If writing about bodily experience is not useful for you, describe the situation or your thoughts instead.

title: What is fear protecting?
blocks: p

Fear can respond to something happening now, to an anticipated outcome, or to something familiar from an earlier experience. An unfamiliar opportunity can be uncomfortable; a familiar situation can still contain a real risk.
p

Rather than asking fear to disappear, ask it to become specific. “This is wrong” can become “I am worried I will be expected to do more than I have agreed to.” The more specific sentence suggests questions about expectations, time and boundaries.
p
You do not need to prove courage by overriding a concern. You also do not need to treat every uncomfortable feeling as a final answer.
bullets
Name the outcome you are afraid of.
Separate what has happened from what you predict might happen.
Identify information, support or a boundary that would matter.
Consider whether waiting or declining is the appropriate next step.
quote
An inquiry is useful when it helps you respond to the concern, not merely rename it.
p

In the hypothetical invitation example, you might ask for the group size and the expected preparation before answering. A clearer agreement may address the concern. It is also possible that, with more information, you will choose to decline.

title: Make the concern specific
blocks: field
I am afraid that...
field
What I know right now is...
field
What I am predicting, remembering or assuming is...
field
The information, support or boundary that would matter is...
field
My next choice is to ask, wait, decline, or take this small step...

title: The image I am protecting
blocks: p

Perhaps you want to be the capable one, the generous one, the person who always knows, or the person who never needs help. These identities can carry values you care about. They can also make some answers difficult to consider.
p
Here, “ego” is a shorthand for investment in a particular image of yourself. It is not an insult, a diagnosis or a reason to distrust every wish you have.
p
Notice when the question moves from “What is happening?” to “What would it mean about me if this were happening?” You may be trying to preserve an identity alongside making a practical decision.
p
For example, someone who values being helpful may agree before considering their capacity. The value is real. So is the need to ask what help they can sustainably offer.
bullets
What do I want this answer to say about me?
What answer would feel embarrassing or disappointing?
Could I remain a person I respect if I changed my mind?
quote
You can protect a value without protecting an unchanging story about yourself.

title: Make room for an honest answer
blocks: field
The person I feel I should be in this situation is...
field
If I admitted uncertainty or changed my mind, I fear it would mean...
field
The value underneath that image might be...
field
A way to honor that value without pretending certainty is...

title: What do I want to be true?
blocks: p
Desire does not make you dishonest. Wanting a relationship, a creative opportunity or a sense of belonging is part of being human. Discernment asks you to give that wanting a name.
p

Consider the difference between “I want this invitation to be right for me” and “The strength of my excitement proves this invitation is right.” The first is an honest wish. The second turns a wish into evidence.
p
You do not need to become indifferent before you can think clearly. You can want something and still ask practical questions about it.
field
What I most want to happen is...
field
If that does not happen, what disappointment would I need to acknowledge?
field
One fact I have been reluctant to consider is...
quote
Name the wish. Let it be a wish. Then return to the question.

title: An impression, held lightly
blocks: p

An intuitive impression may arrive before you have an explanation for it. For the purposes of this workbook, you do not have to decide where the impression came from in order to write it down and examine it.
p

Try holding it in provisional language: “I am noticing a hesitation” or “I have a sense that another question would help.” This preserves the experience without turning it into a declaration about another person or the future.
p

A meaningful impression can still be incomplete. A satisfying coincidence is not, by itself, confirmation of your interpretation. Look at what you can check, and allow a result to change your understanding.
field
The impression, in the simplest language I can use...
field
What would support this interpretation? What would challenge it?
field
What can remain uncertain while I decide how to respond?

title: Four things can be true at once
blocks: p
You might feel excited, afraid, protective of your image, and intuitively hesitant about the same invitation. You do not have to identify one “pure” voice before you can choose a thoughtful response.
field
FEAR / What am I concerned may happen?
field
EGO / What image of myself am I protecting?
field
DESIRE / What do I want to happen?
field
IMPRESSION / What am I noticing before the explanation?
field
When I read these together, the question that deserves attention is...

title: The flattering invitation
blocks: p

The situation: Morgan is invited to lead a small writing gathering. The invitation feels exciting, but the organizer asks for an immediate answer and has not explained the schedule or responsibilities.
p
Observation: there is an invitation, a request for a quick answer and missing information. “They will take advantage of me” is an interpretation, not an established fact.
p

Fear: Morgan worries about agreeing to work they cannot manage.
Ego: being invited feels like proof of being a “real writer.”
Desire: Morgan wants the gathering to be a good opportunity.
Impression: something feels unfinished about saying yes now.
p

A discerning response: “Thank you for thinking of me. Before I decide, could you send the schedule, group size and what you would like me to prepare? I can respond after I have reviewed those details.”
p
This does not establish the organizer’s motives. It turns an uncertain impression into an appropriate request for information. Morgan can still decline if the terms or timing do not fit.
field
What part of Morgan’s situation resembles a question of my own?
note
The point is not that every hesitation means “ask for details.” The response should fit the facts, your capacity and the actual concern.

title: The unanswered message
blocks: p
The situation: Alex sends a personal message to a friend. By the next afternoon there is no reply. Alex has a strong feeling that the friendship is ending.
p
Observation: the message has not received a reply. Alex feels unsettled. Neither fact establishes what the friend thinks.
p

Possible influences: fear of disconnection, a wish for reassurance, and an investment in being the friend who does not need reassurance. The impression may be worth noticing without treating it as knowledge of someone else’s mind.
p

A discerning response: Alex considers the friend’s usual response pattern, waits until an ordinary time to follow up, and asks a direct question if the concern remains. Alex can also decide what level of contact feels workable over time.
p
One delayed reply does not prove an ending. A repeated pattern may still matter. Discernment makes room for both the limits of this single observation and what a larger pattern may reveal.
field
What might Alex check rather than assume?
field
What can Alex choose without knowing the friend’s private thoughts?

title: You do not have to prove a motive
blocks: p
A boundary describes what you will participate in, offer or accept. It does not require a final explanation of someone else’s character.
p

“I cannot take this on this month” makes a different claim from “You are trying to drain my energy.” The first can be true on the basis of your capacity. The second claims knowledge about someone else’s intentions.
p
A boundary may be quiet or uncomfortable. It may disappoint someone. None of those features, by itself, decides whether the boundary is appropriate.
bullets
Name the observable request or situation.
Identify your capacity, preference or limit.
Choose language that states the limit clearly.
Decide what you will do if the request continues.
p

Examples to adapt:
“I need more time before I answer.”
“I can offer one hour, but I cannot take responsibility for the whole event.”
“I am not available for that conversation today.”
quote
A limit can stand without a story about why the other person deserves it.

title: A boundary I can actually use
blocks: field
The request or situation, in observable terms...
field
My capacity, preference or limit...
field
The sentence I could say or write...
field
If the request continues, the action I can take is...
note
Adapt the wording to your circumstances. A script is a starting point, not a requirement to confront someone or explain yourself at length.

title: Learn without forcing certainty
blocks: p
Some decisions need a clear answer now. Others allow a question, a pause or a small step that gives you more information. Look for the scale of response that fits the situation.
p

A useful learning step has a purpose, a limit and a time to review. “I will try harder to trust myself” is difficult to observe. “I will share one paragraph with a trusted reader and ask what they understood” gives you something concrete to learn from.
bullets
What specific question would the step help answer?
How much time, effort or exposure am I choosing?
Can I stop or change course without creating a larger problem?
What result would make me reconsider?
When will I return to review what happened?
p

A small step is not always appropriate. Do not create a risky experiment simply to test whether a concern is “really intuition.” Waiting, declining or seeking relevant advice may be the more thoughtful response.
quote
The next step can be a question. It can also be “not now.”

title: My decision lab
blocks: field
The decision or question...
field
What I know / what I still need to find out...
field
The next step I choose, and what it could help me learn...
field
The limit: what I will not commit to or risk in this step...
field
I will review this on / I will reconsider sooner if...

title: Changing your mind is part of listening
blocks: p
An outcome can teach you something without proving that you were either gifted or foolish. Try to review the specific impression, the interpretation and the action separately.
p

You may have noticed that an agreement was unclear and then incorrectly assumed bad intent. The useful part of the impression was the need for clarity. Revising the explanation does not erase that observation.
p
You may also discover that an impression was mistaken. You can name that plainly. Discernment becomes more useful when there is room for disconfirming information.
bullets
What did I notice before the outcome was known?
What did I predict or assume?
What actually happened?
What remains ambiguous?
What can I learn without making this event prove a story about my identity?
p

When you return to old notes, read what you wrote at the time rather than rewriting the impression to match the result. Keep “I felt uneasy” separate from a more specific prediction you did not actually make.
quote
Self-trust can include the willingness to correct yourself.

title: An honest review
blocks: field
The original impression and interpretation, as I recorded them...
field
The action I took and what actually happened...
field
What supported my interpretation? What did not fit?
field
What remains unknown, and what I would do differently next time...

title: Look across more than one moment
blocks: p

Use this page for brief notes from several separate situations. This is a reflection record, not a score of how intuitive you are. Include missed impressions and ordinary explanations as well as moments that felt meaningful.
field
ENTRY 1 / Date, impression, action, outcome, what I learned...
field
ENTRY 2 / Date, impression, action, outcome, what I learned...
field
ENTRY 3 / Date, impression, action, outcome, what I learned...
field
Across these entries, what pattern deserves another question?

title: Let a symbol ask a question
blocks: p

If tarot or another symbolic practice is part of your spiritual life, you can use it here as a writing prompt. A card, image or phrase can open a question without serving as evidence about another person or a guarantee of an outcome.
p
Choose a card deliberately, draw one if you wish, or select a line from your own writing. You can also skip the symbol and begin with a word such as threshold, belonging or choice.
field
The symbol or phrase I am working with...
field
What does it bring to mind? What story am I connecting to it?
field
What useful question does it open? What does it not establish?
field
What observation or practical question will I return to?

title: A one-page discernment check-in
blocks: p
Use this page again with a new situation. You may answer in a few sentences rather than a full essay.
field
NOTICE / What happened, and what impression arose?
field
SEPARATE / What is observation, and what is interpretation?
field
NAME / What do I fear, want or feel I need to prove?
field
CHECK / What information or conversation would matter?
field
CHOOSE / What boundary, pause or small step fits?
field
RETURN / When will I review this, and what could change my mind?

title: A practice that fits your life
blocks: p
A practice becomes useful when it is small enough to return to. You do not have to write every day or examine every passing feeling. Choose a scale that leaves room for living.
field
The question from this workbook I want to keep close...
field
A situation in which I would like to pause before interpreting...
field
A reminder that would help me be honest about uncertainty...
field
The way I want to use these pages again...
quote
I am noticing something, and I am still learning what it means.

title: Keep a little room open
blocks: p
You do not need to leave these pages with a perfect method for identifying every feeling. You can leave with a more specific question, a clearer boundary or a willingness to look again.
p
You can respect an impression without obeying it immediately. You can acknowledge fear without letting it make every decision. You can want something deeply and still ask what is true.
p
Some questions take time. Some answers change. A listening practice can make room for both.
p
Return to the observation. Name the wish. Ask what can be checked. Choose the next step that fits what you know. Then give yourself permission to learn.
quote
You can listen to yourself and still ask questions.
p
